She is quoting Moses from memory in a Persian palace. Moses had said it to the whole people: chosen above all people on the face of the earth, a special people to himself. Esther is in exile, her people scattered under a foreign king and marked for slaughter, and nothing about that has cancelled what she heard in her tribe. A chosen people stays chosen in the lands of their scattering, and the inheritance is perpetual because the one who gave it does not take it back.
member_note: The Rest of Esther 14:5 — *tookest Yashar'el (Israel) from among all people, and our fathers from all their predecessors, for a perpetual inheritance.* Esther in exile recites what Moses said at Deuteronomy 7:6, a people chosen from among all people, and the choosing holds in the scattering.

apoc_text: For your power stands not in multitude nor your might in strong men: for you are a Yahuah (God) of the afflicted, an helper of the oppressed, an upholder of the weak, a protector of the forlorn, a saviour of them that are without hope.
old_note: Judith 9:11 — *For your power stands not in multitude nor your might in strong men: for you are a Yahuah (God) of the afflicted, an helper of the oppressed, an upholder of the weak, a protector of the forlorn, a saviour of them that are without hope.* Judith confesses the very Helper-of-the-forlorn that Esther leans on, two women with no help but Him.
new_note: *For your power stands not in multitude nor your might in strong men: for you are a Yahuah (God) of the afflicted, an helper of the oppressed, an upholder of the weak, a protector of the forlorn, a saviour of them that are without hope.* (Judith 9:11). *But deliver us with yours hand, and help me that am desolate, and which have no other help but you.* (The Rest of Esther 14:14). Two women, two prayers, the same confession. Judith says Yahuah (God) is the helper of the oppressed and the saviour of those without hope, that his power never stood in numbers or strong men. Esther says it as a plea rather than a creed: deliver us with your hand, help me that am desolate, I have no other help but you. Each one stands alone in front of a power that means to wipe out her people, and each one knows the only hand that can turn it. The strength of Yashar'el (Israel) in both books is a woman on her knees who has run out of every other help.
member_note: Judith 9:11 — *a protector of the forlorn, a saviour of them that are without hope.* Esther prays the same thing at The Rest of Esther 14:14, no other help but you; two women alone before a power bent on their people.

apoc_text: And they said, Behold, we have sent you money to buy you burnt offerings, and sin offerings, and incense, and prepare you manna, and offer upon the altar of Yahuah (God), our Elohim (God);
old_note: Ezra 6:10 — *That they may offer sacrifices of sweet savours unto the Elohim (God) of heaven, and pray for the life of the king, and of his sons.* The Ezra decree binds offerings to prayer-for-the-king exactly as Baruch 1:10 sends silver for burnt offerings while v.11 prays for Nebuchadnezzar.
new_note: *And they said, Behold, we have sent you money to buy you burnt offerings, and sin offerings, and incense, and prepare you manna, and offer upon the altar of Yahuah (God), our Elohim (God); And pray for the life of Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon, and for the life of Balthasar his son, that their days may be upon earth as the days of heaven:* (Baruch 1:10–11). *That they may offer sacrifices of sweet savours unto the Elohim (God) of heaven, and pray for the life of the king, and of his sons.* (Ezra 6:10). The exiles in Babylon sent silver back to Jerusalem for burnt offerings and sin offerings and incense, and in the same breath asked that prayer be made for the life of Nebuchadnezzar and his son. Darius's decree in Ezra does the same two things together: it provides for the sacrifices to the Elohim (God) of heaven and asks that the priests pray for the life of the king and his sons. Offering and prayer for the ruler go together in both, under a Babylonian king and under a Persian one. Jeremiah had told the captives to seek the peace of the city they were carried to and to pray for it (Jeremiah 29:7), and here are the captives doing exactly that, with the altar at the center of it.
member_note: Baruch 1:10 — *we have sent you money to buy you burnt offerings, and sin offerings, and incense.* Offerings and prayer for the king together, as in Darius's decree (Ezra 6:10).
writer_flag: Old note's point (prayer for Nebuchadnezzar) sits in v.11, so 1:10-11 are quoted together and cited as Baruch 1:10-11.

apoc_text: O Jerusalem, look about you toward the east, and behold the joy that comes to you from Yahuah (God).
old_note: Isaiah 49:18 — *Lift up thine eyes round about, and behold: all these gather themselves together, and come to thee. As I live, saith Yahuah (LORD), thou shalt surely clothe thee with them all, as with an ornament, and bind them on thee, as a bride doeth.* Baruch 4:36's call to Jerusalem to look and behold the coming joy is Isaiah's lift-up-thine-eyes upon the gathering children.
new_note: *O Jerusalem, look about you toward the east, and behold the joy that comes to you from Yahuah (God).* (Baruch 4:36). *Lift up thine eyes round about, and behold: all these gather themselves together, and come to thee. As I live, saith Yahuah (LORD), thou shalt surely clothe thee with them all, as with an ornament, and bind them on thee, as a bride doeth.* (Isaiah 49:18). Baruch tells Jerusalem to look east and behold the joy coming to her; Isaiah tells her to lift up her eyes round about and behold her children gathering and coming to her, so many she will wear them like a bride's ornaments. The same city is told to look up in both, and what she sees is the same: her own children coming back. Isaiah swears it by the life of Yahuah (LORD). Baruch, writing from the captivity, is holding Isaiah's promise up for the exiles to see.
member_note: Baruch 4:36 — *behold the joy that comes to you from Yahuah (God).* Isaiah's lift up thine eyes upon the gathering children (Isaiah 49:18).

apoc_text: For my hope is in the Everlasting, that he will save you; and joy is come to me from the Holy One, because of the mercy which shall soon come to you from the Everlasting our Saviour.
old_note: Isaiah 66:13 — *As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you; and ye shall be comforted in Jerusalem.* The joy-from-the-Holy-One of Baruch 4:22 is Yahuah's mother-comfort poured out in Jerusalem.
new_note: *For my hope is in the Everlasting, that he will save you; and joy is come to me from the Holy One, because of the mercy which shall soon come to you from the Everlasting our Saviour.* (Baruch 4:22). *As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you; and ye shall be comforted in Jerusalem.* (Isaiah 66:13). Jerusalem speaks here as a mother whose children were carried off, and she tells them her hope: the Everlasting will save them, and joy has already come to her from the Holy One because of the mercy soon coming. Isaiah had promised that Yahuah (God) would comfort his people as a mother comforts, and that they would be comforted in Jerusalem. The mother's joy in Baruch and the mother's comfort in Isaiah are one promise, told from the city's side and from the side of Yahuah (God). The comfort is the children coming home; the chapter ends with them gathered from east to west (Baruch 4:37).
member_note: Baruch 4:22 — *joy is come to me from the Holy One, because of the mercy which shall soon come.* The mother's comfort of Isaiah 66:13, told from Jerusalem's side.

apoc_text: This is the book of the commandments of Yahuah (God), and the law that endureth for ever: all they that keep it shall come to life; but such as leave it shall die.
old_note: Deuteronomy 30:14 — *But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it.* The commandment is not far off but near and keepable, exactly the take-hold-of-it nearness Baruch 4:1-2 presses.
new_note: *This is the book of the commandments of Yahuah (God), and the law that endureth for ever: all they that keep it shall come to life; but such as leave it shall die. Turn you, O Jacob, and take hold of it: walk in the presence of the light thereof, that you may be illuminated.* (Baruch 4:1–2). *But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it.* (Deuteronomy 30:14). Baruch sets the book of the commandments before Jacob and says take hold of it, walk in its light. Moses had said the same about the same book: the word is not up in heaven or across the sea, it is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it (Deuteronomy 30:11–14). Both speak of the Torah as a thing within reach, not an impossible standard set up to show failure but a lamp handed to a people to walk by. Baruch's turn you, O Jacob, and take hold of it is Moses's that thou mayest do it, spoken again to the exiles.

The many of the broad way are the many of this world; the few of the narrow way are the few of the world to come. The numbers match because the two men are describing the same thing.

apoc_text: Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.
old_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you. If you have abundance give alms accordingly: if you have but a little, be not afraid to give according to that little.* (Tobit 4:7-8). Tobit's charge to his son is the cheerful giver before the letter: give *let not your eye be envious* — the opposite of *grudgingly, or of necessity* — and give *according as he purposeth in his heart,* whether of abundance or of little. This is the heart-posture Paul commands and Elohim (God) loves (2 Corinthians 9:7), with the same promise that the giver's own face is not turned away from the favour of the Most High.
new_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you. If you have abundance give alms accordingly: if you have but a little, be not afraid to give according to that little:* (Tobit 4:7–8). *Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for Elohim (God) loveth a cheerful giver.* (2 Corinthians 9:7). Tobit's son is told to give without an envious eye, out of abundance or out of a little. Paul says the same to Corinth: not grudgingly, not of necessity, each as he purposes in his heart, for Elohim (God) loves a cheerful giver. The heart that gives gladly is the heart the library had been shaping for generations before the letter. Paul was not writing a new ethic for a new people; he was writing Tobit's charge to the scattered children of Yashar'el (Israel) who had grown up among the nations and forgotten it.
member_note: Tobit 4:7 — *when you give alms, let not your eye be envious.* Give of abundance or of little, without the envious eye; *not grudgingly, or of necessity* (2 Corinthians 9:7).

apoc_text: For she is the breath of the power of Yahuah (God), and a pure influence flowing from the glory of the Almighty: therefore can no defiled thing fall into her.
old_note: *For she is the breath of the power of Yahuah (God), and a pure influence flowing from the glory of the Almighty: therefore can no defiled thing fall into her.* (Wisdom 7:25). The Hebrew library beheld Wisdom as *the breath of the power of Yahuah (God), and a pure influence flowing from the glory of the Almighty* — brought forth from the One, sharing his glory, yet not a second God beside him. This is the same posture as the Formed who was *in the form of Elohim (God)* (Philippians 2:6): the glory flows out FROM the Almighty into the One brought forth. Read as the Formed, Wisdom's breath-of-the-power is the Son who carries the Father's glory as the One emptied and exalted, not a co-equal rival to the Father.
new_note: *For she is the breath of the power of Yahuah (God), and a pure influence flowing from the glory of the Almighty: therefore can no defiled thing fall into her.* (Wisdom of Solomon 7:25). *Who, being in the form of Elohim (God), thought it not robbery to be equal with Elohim (God):* (Philippians 2:6). The Hebrew library saw Wisdom as the breath of the power of Yahuah (God), a pure influence flowing from the glory of the Almighty. Brought forth from him, carrying his glory, and not a second god standing beside him. Paul describes the same one as being in the form of Elohim (God) and counting it no robbery to be equal with Elohim (God), and then in the next breath emptying himself. What flows from the glory is of the glory, so the equality is no theft; and what flows has a source, so he has a Father and takes the lower place freely. The Formed is not a rival to the Formless; he is what the Formless breathed out.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 7:25 — *the breath of the power of Yahuah (God), and a pure influence flowing from the glory of the Almighty.* The breath of the power flowing from the glory is the one in the form of Elohim (God) (Philippians 2:6), brought forth, not a rival.

apoc_text: He created me from the beginning before the world, and I shall never fail.
old_note: *He created me from the beginning before the world, and I shall never fail.* (Sirach 24:9). The library's Wisdom speaks of being *created from the beginning before the world* — brought forth before the ages, present when *the Creator of all things gave me a commandment* (Sirach 24:8). It is the same pre-creation pre-eminence the hymn ascribes to the Son: *by him were all things created... and he is before all things, and by him all things consist* (Colossians 1:16-17). Read as the Formed (not a second co-equal Elohim), this Wisdom-before-the-world is the firstborn-Heir brought forth before the works, through whom the all-things were made.
new_note: *He created me from the beginning before the world, and I shall never fail.* (Ecclesiasticus 24:9). *For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him:* (Colossians 1:16). Wisdom says she was brought forth from the beginning, before the world, and that she will never fail. Paul says of the Son that all things in heaven and earth were created by him and for him — he is before all things, and everything holds together in him. These are one and the same: the Wisdom beside the Maker before the world is the Formed one through whom the all things were made, the Son who has a Father and is before every creature. Not a second co-equal Elohim (God) beside the Father, but the Word the Father brought forth, who came in flesh as Yahusha (Jesus).
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 24:9 — *He created me from the beginning before the world, and I shall never fail.* Wisdom before the world is the Son by whom all things were created (Colossians 1:16).

apoc_text: Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.
old_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you* (Tobit 4:7). Tobit's charge to give alms and *turn not your face from any poor* is the open-handed care Paul orders the believing household to extend to its widows: *If any man or woman that believeth have widows, let them relieve them, and let not the church be charged; that it may relieve them that are widows indeed* (1 Timothy 5:16). The believer relieves his own widows so the assembly's care is kept for the truly desolate — the same generosity the library blesses, the face never turned from the poor.
new_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* (Tobit 4:7). *If any man or woman that believeth have widows, let them relieve them, and let not the church be charged; that it may relieve them that are widows indeed.* (1 Timothy 5:16). Tobit's charge is to turn his face from no poor man. Paul orders the believing household to relieve its own widows, so that the assembly's care is kept for the widows who have no one. Both put the first duty of mercy at home, in the household, before it goes out the door. The face never turned from the poor begins with the poor who are nearest.
member_note: Tobit 4:7 — *neither turn your face from any poor.* The household relieves its own widows first (1 Timothy 5:16), the face never turned from the nearest poor.

apoc_text: All these things are the book of the covenant of the most high Yahuah (God), even the law which Moses commanded for an heritage to the congregations of Jacob.
old_note: *All these things are the book of the covenant of the most high Yahuah (God), even the law which Moses commanded for an heritage to the congregations of Jacob* (Sirach 24:23). Here the restored witness names plainly what Psalm 19 has been praising: the Wisdom sweeter than honey IS *the law which Moses commanded for an heritage*. The Torah whose keeping holds *great reward* (Psalm 19:11) is *the book of the covenant of the most high Yahuah*, the inheritance of the congregations — Red Line #6 spoken outright: the law is the heritage, never the curse.
new_note: *All these things are the book of the covenant of the most high Yahuah (God), even the law which Moses commanded for an heritage to the congregations of Jacob.* (Ecclesiasticus 24:23). *Moreover by them is thy servant warned: and in keeping of them there is great reward.* (Psalm 19:11). David spent a whole psalm praising the law of Yahuah (God), sweeter than honey, warning his servant, holding great reward for the one who keeps it. Sirach names what David was praising: the Wisdom whose memorial is sweeter than honey is *the law which Moses commanded for an heritage*. The Torah is the inheritance of the congregations of Jacob, the book of the covenant of the most high Yahuah (God). It is the heritage, not the curse, and the one who keeps it finds the great reward the psalmist promised.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 24:23 — *the law which Moses commanded for an heritage to the congregations of Jacob.* The Wisdom sweeter than honey is the Torah, the inheritance whose keeping holds *great reward* (Psalm 19:11).

apoc_text: Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.
old_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* (Tobit 4:7). Paul tells Titus to teach the believers a settled habit of usefulness: *let ours also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful* (Titus 3:14). Tobit's charge — *Give alms of your substance... turn not your face from any poor* — is the same fruitful, neighbour-serving good work, the doing of mercy that the law commands and the new heart loves.
new_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* (Tobit 4:7). *And let ours also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful.* (Titus 3:14). Paul tells Titus to teach the believers a settled habit of usefulness: maintain good works for necessary uses, and so bear fruit. Tobit's charge is one of those works named exactly — give alms of what you have, turn your face from no poor man. This is the doing of mercy the Torah commands and the new heart loves, and the library had been teaching it to sons in exile long before Paul wrote to Crete.
member_note: Tobit 4:7 — *let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor.* The good work for necessary uses that keeps the believer from being unfruitful (Titus 3:14).

apoc_text: For you layest up a good treasure for thyself against the day of necessity.
old_note: *For you layest up a good treasure for thyself against the day of necessity.* (Tobit 4:9). Tobit charges his son to do good works as a treasure laid up: *Give alms of your substance... If you have abundance give alms accordingly: if you have but a little, be not afraid to give... For you layest up a good treasure for thyself against the day of necessity* (Tobit 4:7-9). This is the very posture Paul commends — *that they which have believed in Elohim (God) might be careful to maintain good works... good and profitable unto men* (Titus 3:8) — the obedient, open-handed life that flows from a heart that fears Yahuah (God) and keeps his commandments (Tobit 4:5).
new_note: *For you layest up a good treasure for thyself against the day of necessity.* (Tobit 4:9). *This is a faithful saying, and these things I will that thou affirm constantly, that they which have believed in Elohim (God) might be careful to maintain good works. These things are good and profitable unto men.* (Titus 3:8). Tobit's son is told to give alms as treasure laid up against the day of need, out of a heart that fears Yahuah (God) and keeps his commandments (4:5). Paul tells Titus to affirm constantly that those who have believed be careful to maintain good works, good and profitable to men. The two are one posture: believing and doing are not rivals, and the open hand is what a believing heart does. The library had been teaching that to sons in exile long before the letter.
member_note: Tobit 4:9 — *you layest up a good treasure for thyself against the day of necessity.* Alms as good works laid up, the fruit of a believing heart careful to maintain them (Titus 3:8).

apoc_text: All these things are the book of the covenant of the most high Yahuah (God), even the law which Moses commanded for an heritage to the congregations of Jacob.
old_note: *All these things are the book of the covenant of the most high Yahuah (God), even the law which Moses commanded for an heritage to the congregations of Jacob* (Sirach 24:23). Wisdom is named outright as the Torah, the heritage of Jacob — the same word *shewed unto Jacob, his statutes and his judgments unto Yashar'el (Israel)* (Psalm 147:19). The law Moses commanded is *an heritage to the congregations of Jacob*: the covenant inheritance no other nation received, Red Line #6 spoken plainly.
new_note: *All these things are the book of the covenant of the most high Yahuah (God), even the law which Moses commanded for an heritage to the congregations of Jacob.* (Ecclesiasticus 24:23). *He sheweth his word unto Jacob, his statutes and his judgments unto Yashar'el (Israel).* (Psalm 147:19). Sirach says it without a veil: Wisdom is the book of the covenant, the law Moses commanded as the heritage of Jacob. The psalmist had already sung that Yahuah (God) shows his word to Jacob and his statutes and judgments to Yashar'el (Israel), and the next verse of that psalm says he did not deal so with any nation. The Torah is an inheritance handed to one family, the congregations of Jacob, and an inheritance is a gift to a son, not a burden laid on a slave. The law is the heritage of Yashar'el (Israel), never the curse.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 24:23 — *the law which Moses commanded for an heritage to the congregations of Jacob.* Wisdom named as the Torah, the heritage of Jacob; the word, statutes and judgments shown to Yashar'el (Israel) at Psalm 147:19.

apoc_text: Remember the commandments, and bear no malice to your neighbour: remember the covenant of the Highest, and wink at ignorance.
old_note: Sirach 28:7 — *Remember the commandments, and bear no malice to your neighbour: remember the covenant of the Highest, and wink at ignorance.* To forgive even the shameless and bear no grudge is Ben Sira's no-malice-to-thy-neighbour, rooted in the commandments.
new_note: *Remember the commandments, and bear no malice to your neighbour: remember the covenant of the Highest, and wink at ignorance.* (Ecclesiasticus 28:7). *But if he be shameless and persisteth in his wrong-doing, even so forgive him from the heart, and leave to Elohim (God) the avenging.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 100:7). Sirach says remember the commandments and bear no malice to your neighbour, and overlook what was done in ignorance. The patriarch's testament goes further down the same road: even if the man is shameless and keeps on in his wrong, forgive him from the heart and leave the avenging to Elohim (God). Both are the commandment of Leviticus 19:18 lived out, no vengeance and no grudge. Forgiving the shameless is simply bearing no malice when it costs the most.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 28:7 — *Remember the commandments, and bear no malice to your neighbour.* No malice rooted in the commandments; the Testaments say *even so forgive him from the heart, and leave to Elohim (God) the avenging*.

apoc_text: Believe in him, and he will help you; order your way aright, and trust in him.
old_note: *Believe in him, and he will help you; order your way aright, and trust in him* (Sirach 2:6). *Trust in Yahuah (LORD), and do good* (Psalm 37:3): the son of Sirach repeats the psalm's counsel — believe, order the way aright, trust — the same trust-and-do-good walk that leans the whole life on Yahuah's help.
new_note: *Believe in him, and he will help you; order your way aright, and trust in him.* (Ecclesiasticus 2:6). *Trust in Yahuah (LORD), and do good; so shalt thou dwell in the land, and verily thou shalt be fed.* (Psalm 37:3). Sirach is repeating David. Believe in him, order your way aright, trust in him, is the same counsel as trust in Yahuah (LORD) and do good, the trusting and the doing bound together in one breath. Neither verse lets a man trust Yahuah (God) while walking however he pleases, and neither lets him order his way as if his own ordering were what held him up. The whole life leans on his help, and the leaning shows up as a way set aright.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 2:6 — *Believe in him, and he will help you; order your way aright, and trust in him.* David's *Trust in Yahuah (LORD), and do good* (Psalm 37:3), repeated.

apoc_text: Give Yahuah (God) his honour with a good eye, and diminish not the firstfruits of yours hands.
old_note: *Give Yahuah (God) his honour with a good eye, and diminish not the firstfruits of yours hands* (Sirach 35:8). The restored witness keeps the proverb exactly: *Honour Yahuah (LORD) with thy substance, and with the firstfruits* (Proverbs 3:9) is *Give Yahuah (God) his honour with a good eye, and diminish not the firstfruits of yours hands*. The firstfruits are not to be cut short; the honour of Yahuah is shown in the unstinted giving of the first and best.
new_note: *Give Yahuah (God) his honour with a good eye, and diminish not the firstfruits of yours hands.* (Ecclesiasticus 35:8). *Honour Yahuah (LORD) with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase:* (Proverbs 3:9). Sirach is repeating Solomon almost word for word. Honour Yahuah (LORD) with what you have and with your firstfruits, Solomon says; give Yahuah (God) his honour and do not diminish the firstfruits of your hands, says Sirach, and he adds the good eye, the ungrudging eye, as the manner of it. The first and the best belong to Yahuah (God), and they are not to be cut short. The proverb came down whole, and Sirach handed it on whole.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 35:8 — *diminish not the firstfruits of yours hands.* Proverbs 3:9's firstfruits, kept whole and given with a good eye.

apoc_text: Come to me, all you that be desirous of me, and fill yourselves with my fruits.
old_note: *Come to me, all you that be desirous of me, and fill yourselves with my fruits* (Sirach 24:19). Wisdom's invitation parallels the prophet's: *Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters... come ye, buy, and eat* (Isaiah 55:1) — the same come-and-be-filled call, all the desirous bidden to come and eat freely of what satisfies.
new_note: *Come to me, all you that be desirous of me, and fill yourselves with my fruits.* (Ecclesiasticus 24:19). *Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.* (Isaiah 55:1). Wisdom calls everyone who wants her to come and fill themselves; the prophet calls everyone who thirsts to come to the waters and eat without money. Both invitations go out to the desirous and the thirsty, and both offer what satisfies for nothing but the coming. There is no price at the door in either verse, only the call to come and be filled.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 24:19 — *Come to me, all you that be desirous of me.* Wisdom's invitation stands beside Isaiah 55:1, *come ye, buy, and eat*; the same free call to come and be filled.

apoc_text: And left him not in bonds, till she brought him the sceptre of the kingdom, and power against those that oppressed him: as for them that had accused him, she shewed them to be liars, and gave him perpetual glory.
old_note: *And left him not in bonds, till she brought him the sceptre of the kingdom, and power against those that oppressed him: as for them that had accused him, she shewed them to be liars, and gave him perpetual glory* (Wisdom of Solomon 10:14). *He made him lord of his house, and ruler of all his substance: To bind his princes at his pleasure; and teach his senators wisdom* (Psalm 105:21-22): the same exaltation — not left in bonds but brought the sceptre of the kingdom, given power over his oppressors; the sold-and-bound one raised to rule and to teach wisdom.
new_note: *And left him not in bonds, till she brought him the sceptre of the kingdom, and power against those that oppressed him: as for them that had accused him, she shewed them to be liars, and gave him perpetual glory.* (Wisdom of Solomon 10:14). *He made him lord of his house, and ruler of all his substance:* (Psalm 105:21). Joseph was sold, went down into the pit, and was not left in bonds. Wisdom says she brought him the sceptre of the kingdom and power against those that oppressed him, showed his accusers to be liars, and gave him perpetual glory. The psalm tells it as history: Pharaoh made him lord of his house and ruler of all he had, and the next verse adds that he bound Pharaoh's princes at his pleasure and taught his senators wisdom (Psalm 105:22). The bound man binds the princes; the man accused as a liar is the one who ends up teaching the court. Wisdom went down into the pit with him and came up with him to the throne.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 10:14 — *left him not in bonds, till she brought him the sceptre of the kingdom.* Joseph, not left in bonds but made lord of Pharaoh's house (Psalm 105:21), is the sold man raised to the sceptre.

apoc_text: Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.
old_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you* (Tobit 4:7). The exile-righteous Tobit lives the Mishpat among the nations: the open hand to the poor is the same mercy the Torah commands in *Thou shalt neither vex a stranger, nor oppress him* (Exodus 22:21). The promise mirrors the warning — turn not thy face from the poor, and Yahuah turns not His from thee.
new_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* (Tobit 4:7). *Thou shalt neither vex a stranger, nor oppress him: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.* (Exodus 22:21). Tobit lives in Nineveh, a stranger among the nations, and he teaches his son the open hand to the poor. The Torah had told Yashar'el (Israel) not to vex or oppress the stranger, because they had been strangers in Egypt. Tobit is now the stranger, and he keeps the commandment from the other side of it, showing mercy where he might have asked for it. The promise mirrors the warning: turn not your face from the poor, and Yahuah (God) turns not his from you.
member_note: Tobit 4:7 — *neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* The stranger in Nineveh keeps the mercy Torah commanded toward the stranger (Exodus 22:21).

apoc_text: Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.
old_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* (Tobit 4:7) — old Yashar'el (Israel) taught its sons this very secret-handed giving.
new_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* (Tobit 4:7). *Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven.* (Matthew 6:1). Tobit ties alms to one face, the face of Yahuah (God) turned toward the giver. Yahusha (Jesus) warns against alms done to be seen of men, because a gift aimed at men's eyes has already had its reward and the Father's is lost. Both are saying whose face the giver should be looking for. Tobit never mentions secrecy, but he sets the giver before the Father's face and no one else's, and that is the whole of the warning in Matthew.
member_note: Tobit 4:7 — *the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* Alms given for the Father's face, not for men's eyes (Matthew 6:1).
writer_flag: Corrected the old note: it called Tobit 4:7 'secret-handed giving', but the verse says nothing about secrecy. The real link is whose face the giver seeks (the Father's, not men's).

apoc_text: Many have sinned for a small matter; and he that seeks for abundance will turn his eyes away.
old_note: *Many have sinned for a small matter; and he that seeks for abundance will turn his eyes away* (Ecclesiasticus 27:1). Ephraim's boast — *Yet I am become rich, I have found me out substance: in all my labours they shall find none iniquity in me* (Hosea 12:8) — is the very self-blinding Sirach names: *he that seeks for abundance will turn his eyes away*. The pursuit of gain hides the sin from the sinner's own sight.
new_note: *Many have sinned for a small matter; and he that seeks for abundance will turn his eyes away.* (Ecclesiasticus 27:1). *And Ephraim said, Yet I am become rich, I have found me out substance: in all my labours they shall find none iniquity in me that were sin.* (Hosea 12:8). Ephraim had grown rich and could find no sin in any of his labours, and Sirach tells you how that happens: the one who is chasing abundance turns his eyes away from the small matters he sinned in to get it. The gain does not remove the sin. It hides the sin from the man who did it, until he can stand in the prophet's hearing and swear his hands are clean. That blindness is what Hosea is prophesying against, and it is what Sirach is warning the reader of before it sets in.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 27:1 — *he that seeks for abundance will turn his eyes away.* The blindness of Ephraim's boast at Hosea 12:8, *they shall find none iniquity in me*; the pursuit of gain hides the sin from the sinner.

apoc_text: He that revengeth shall find vengeance from Yahuah (God), and he will surely keep his sins in remembrance.
old_note: *He that revengeth shall find vengeance from Yahuah (God), and he will surely keep his sins in remembrance* (Ecclesiasticus 28:1). The sage of Sirach echoes Abigail's plea word for word in substance — the one who takes his own vengeance is himself overtaken by it. Abigail spares David from that snare: *Yahuah (LORD) hath withholden thee from coming to shed blood, and from avenging thyself with thine own hand* (1 Samuel 25:26).
new_note: *He that revengeth shall find vengeance from Yahuah (God), and he will surely keep his sins in remembrance.* (Ecclesiasticus 28:1). *Now therefore, my lord, as Yahuah (LORD) liveth, and as thy soul liveth, seeing Yahuah (LORD) hath withholden thee from coming to shed blood, and from avenging thyself with thine own hand, now let thine enemies, and they that seek evil to my lord, be as Nabal.* (1 Samuel 25:26). Abigail met David on the road while he was riding to shed Nabal's blood, and she told him plainly that Yahuah (LORD) had held him back from avenging himself with his own hand. Sirach says why that mattered: the man who takes his own vengeance finds vengeance from Yahuah (God), and his sins are kept in remembrance. David was one hour from writing that sentence against himself, and a wise woman turned him from it. He blessed her for it, and Nabal died by the hand of Yahuah (God) ten days later without David lifting a finger.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 28:1 — *He that revengeth shall find vengeance from Yahuah (God).* The snare Abigail turned David from at 1 Samuel 25:26, *avenging thyself with thine own hand*.

old_note: Numbers 18:7 — *Therefore thou and thy sons with thee shall keep your priest’s office for every thing of the altar, and within the vail; and ye shall serve: I have given your priest’s office unto you as a service of gift: and the stranger that cometh nigh shall be put to death.* The one-in-a-year, high-priest-only access Ptolemy is told of is the Torah's standing penalty against any stranger pressing within the vail.
new_note: *And when they told him that this was not permissible, none of the nation, no, nor even the priests in general, but only the supreme high priest of all, and he only once in a year, being allowed to go in, he would by no means give way.* (3 Maccabees 1:11). *Therefore thou and thy sons with thee shall keep your priest’s office for every thing of the altar, and within the vail; and ye shall serve: I have given your priest’s office unto you as a service of gift: and the stranger that cometh nigh shall be put to death.* (Numbers 18:7). Ptolemy saw the temple, admired it, and decided he would walk into the sanctuary itself. The priests told him the rule: no one of the nation, not even the priests, only the high priest, and he only once a year. The king called that an honour he was being denied; the Torah calls it a death sentence for anyone else who comes near. Yahuah (God) gave the priesthood to Aaron and his sons as a gift, within the vail as well as at the altar, and said the stranger that cometh nigh shall be put to death. The high priest's one entry a year on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:2) was not a privilege to be extended; it was the boundary Yahuah (God) set on his own dwelling, and Ptolemy was pressing against the boundary and its penalty.
